passage:
Kabir had spoken to Sarita exactly four times, but on the bus home he could already picture the two of them at a rooftop cafe next year, laughing about a trip they had not yet taken. She was funny and sure of herself, quick with a joke in the lecture hall, and he filled in everything else himself.

When she posted a story about a stray puppy, he replied at once, then deleted the message and wrote a shorter one. On Thursday he typed, "Coffee sometime?" and then stared at the screen. Her answer came three hours later and he read it six times. "Sounds good! Saturday?" Was that enthusiasm or politeness? He put his phone face down, then picked it up again to check the time she had answered.

After a month of Saturdays, he learned other things. Sarita was often late and cancelled plans without saying sorry. She got sharp when she was tired and talked over waiters. She also read to her grandmother every Sunday. Her views on money and family were not always his.

"So what do I like?" he asked Dolma at the canteen. "How I feel when we text, or the person she really is?" Dolma shrugged and smiled. "Only you know."

qa.q: How many times had Kabir spoken to Sarita before picturing the rooftop cafe?
qa.a: He had spoken to her four times.

qa.q: How did Kabir's picture of Sarita on the bus differ from what he learned after a month of Saturdays, and how did his question change?
qa.a: At first he filled in everything else himself, but later he saw her lateness, sharp moods and differing views, and his question turned from how the feelings felt to whether he liked the real person.

qa.q: What was Kabir feeling as he read her reply six times?
qa.a: He felt anxious and unsure, afraid of rejection, and treated the reply time and wording as very important.

qa.q: What could Kabir do next to answer his own question about Sarita?
qa.a: He could keep seeing her in ordinary situations and talk honestly about what matters to each of them, then decide based on the person he sees.

grounding: Three early stages from attraction to commitment: idealising a classmate, nervously approaching her, and getting to know the real person as the glow fades.
